frase_gancho.texto: A wall of serpents that devour warriors.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the wall of serpents, move on to another wall in the same city, where instead of reptiles, jaguars, coyotes, and eagles parade past: the emblems of the warriors of Tula.

guion_corto.texto: In front of you is a section of the Coatepantli, the “Wall of Serpents” of Tula, which surrounded the sacred space next to Pyramid B. Its stone slabs, with traces of red, blue, and yellow, show an enormous rattlesnake moving horizontally. From its open mouth a fleshless figure half emerges: you can see the skull, the ribs, and perhaps an arm holding a weapon. Above, the wall was crowned with crenellations shaped like a cut shell. The image is harsh, but it is not only punishment. It is interpreted that being swallowed by the serpent was a transformation: the warrior left his body behind and was reborn in the sky, at the side of the Sun.

guion_largo.texto:
“Coatepantli” is a Nahuatl word that is easy to understand: coatl, serpent, and tepantli, wall. It is the name the Mexica gave, centuries later, to this kind of wall, and archaeologists adopted it for the one at Tula. Don’t picture the rampart of a besieged city. This wall did not stop armies: it separated. On the inside lay the sacred space, with Pyramid B, the Palacio Quemado, and the ball court; on the outside, the city of everyday life.

Look closely at the scene. The serpent is not the harmless reptile that crawls among the stones: it is a fantastic animal, a rattlesnake, with its body covered in scrolls that suggest feathers and scales at the same time. From its jaws emerges half of a human body reduced to bone. This is no ordinary victim: he carries a weapon, and that is why he is thought to be a warrior. It is an image of devouring, but also of passage.

Remember the [disc of death](mna_s04_disco_muerte) in the Teotihuacán Hall: there, the Earth swallowed the Sun so that it could be reborn. Here, the serpent swallows the warrior for the same reason. For the peoples of Mesoamerica, death in combat was not a failure: it was a way of joining the cycle of the Sun and accompanying it on its path. The serpent is the door. What goes in as bone comes out a star.

Notice the crown of the wall. The crenellations shaped like a cut shell are a very frequently repeated symbol: it is the ehecacózcatl, the “jewel of the wind,” emblem of Ehécatl, the god of the wind. If you remember the bronze shell in the pond of the courtyard, it is the same symbol. In Tula, those shells crowned the wall and gave it an air of rhythm and festivity, like a stone crest against the sky.

The wall preserves traces of color: red, blue, and yellow. In its day it must have looked bright from a distance, like almost all the architecture of Mesoamerica. Today the stone looks gray and rough, but when the city was alive, the fleshless warriors and the serpents were vividly colored. Seeing a wall of bones painted red and blue is a good lesson: what is gloomy to us was bright and full of hope to them.

Archaeologists, among them Jorge Acosta in the forties and fifties, found the panels lying at the foot of the pyramid, among ashes, after the city burned around one thousand one hundred fifty. They reconstructed it at the site of Tula, and one section is displayed here. Walls of serpents had a long life: the Mexica surrounded the sacred precinct of Tenochtitlan with one, and the one at Tenayuca, in the State of Mexico, still survives.

And there is one last thread. In Mexica tradition, Coatepec, the “hill of the serpent,” was the place where Huitzilopochtli, the god of the Sun and of war, was born, and it was said to be near Tula. The Templo Mayor of Tenochtitlan represented that hill. In the Mexica Hall you will see his defeated sister, [Coyolxauhqui](mna_s06_coyolxauhqui), at the foot of that mountain. The serpent of Tula and the one of the Templo Mayor are kin.

That is why it is worth looking at this wall as a boundary and also as a door: a boundary between the ordinary world and the sacred one, and a door between life and what comes after.

texto: Find the serpent’s head and the figure emerging from its jaws
Look closely at the crenellations shaped like a cut shell
Discover the traces of red, blue, and yellow that remain on the stone

texto.Material: Basalt carved in low relief and incision, originally polychrome
texto.Origin: Tula, Hidalgo (Wall of Serpents, rear face of Pyramid B)
texto.Dimensions: Individual slab: 32.3 cm high x 105 cm wide x 5.5 cm thick

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Coatepantli was a defensive wall to protect the city from enemies.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Its main function is thought to have been symbolic: it marked the boundary of the sacred space and decorated it with images of war and transformation.
